store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's a thrilling time for me as a student.
store.1: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to for a while. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's a thrilling time for me as a student.
store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theoretical aspects of problem-solving, particularly in areas like pathfinding in large networks and handling huge datasets efficiently. We've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor's intuitive explanations make these complex concepts more accessible. She'll present a seemingly insurmountable problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Leaving that class always leaves me with a buzzing mind, eager to tackle more challenges.
store.3: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is another challenging class. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself, as we have to collaborate with individuals who have different coding styles and ideas about the final product. This is a great way to learn how to integrate code with others, handle concurrency issues, and ensure smooth operation even in the face of node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in a config file. However, once we fixed that issue and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.4: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which is a must-have for me as a gamer at heart. The professor is from the industry and has worked on some indie games that did well. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and I had a blast designing a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept. The challenge was finding the perfect balance between difficulty and player satisfaction. It was rewarding to see the design come together and knowing that I had created something enjoyable for players. This class is a highlight of my semester.
store.5: I have to admit that I initially felt intimidated by the Introduction to Quantum Computing class, but it's turned out to be a fascinating course. The professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than just math, which makes it more accessible. We're using code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits, which helps to illustrate the theoretical benefits of quantum algorithms like Grover's and Shor's. It's mind-blowing to see how these algorithms can outperform classical methods. This class has made me rethink how I approach problems and has opened my eyes to the potential of quantum computing.
store.6: The Capstone Project course is definitely the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.7: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it explores interesting connections between consciousness, the concept of mind, and artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have in-depth discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding-intensive nature of my other classes. It's fascinating to analyze abstract ideas and consider the ethical implications of building AI systems that could potentially mimic or simulate human thinking. I recently wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. This topic is highly debated in the philosophy world, and researching it was a thought-provoking experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this class provides me with that perspective.
store.8: My typical college schedule is quite packed, especially on Mondays and Wednesdays. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be challenging if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open for assignments, group projects, or labs. I also make time for undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm managing to stay on top of everything so far, but it's a tight squeeze.
store.9: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone consumes around ten hours a week, and it can easily go up to 20 hours if we encounter any major issues or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week to discuss progress and assign tasks. We also rely heavily on Slack and Discord to stay updated on each other's work. Coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned so far and push the boundaries of what's possible.
store.10: I'm having a blast this semester. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's not as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway from my four years is that I've learned to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
